content: The World Health Organization (WHO) in 2014 developed consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations. These guidelines were informed by the experiences and challenges faced by transgender individuals, particularly regarding access to gender-affirming care. A 31-year-old transgender man from the United States described his struggle with transitioning, stating, I had three options: I could kill myself, which was an option. I could go back to my home country and try to figure out how to transition there, or I could transition here. He highlighted the mental toll of navigating these decisions. A 36-year-old transgender woman from El Salvador expressed her distress over the lack of access to hormone therapy, saying, If I had the opportunity to take hormone treatment, maybe my breasts and body would look different, and I would feel more comfortable with my gender identity and appearance. Sometimes I feel very sad and depressed because the way people see you is the way they treat you. I feel very uncomfortable that I don’t have the support or a doctor to help me with hormone treatment to align my body with my gender identity. There are times I look in the mirror and think about ending my life. A 29-year-old transgender woman from Thailand shared the positive physical changes she experienced with hormone therapy: The hormones changed a lot. My skin became smoother, and the shape of my face has completely changed. I have small breasts now, and my skin has become more feminine. Access to hormone therapy was identified as one of the most significant health challenges faced by transgender individuals. Many interviewees reported a lack of information and guidance from healthcare systems and medical professionals. Barriers included high costs, lengthy and complicated processes, and intrusive questioning. Some individuals reported no access to hormones through the healthcare system at all. A 36-year-old transgender woman from the Philippines noted, It’s trial and error because endocrinologists didn’t study hormone replacement therapy in medical school. It’s an experimental phase for them to see what works and what doesn’t, and patients have to bear the consequences of this experimental phase. Stigma and discrimination from healthcare professionals were common experiences when transgender individuals sought hormone therapy. A 31-year-old transgender man from the Russian Federation shared, I was supervised by a psychiatrist who was trying to change my mind. My doctor believed she could help me reconcile with my birth sex. Due to these challenges, many transgender individuals resorted to self-medicating with hormones. This often involved purchasing oral contraceptive pills from local pharmacies or obtaining injectable hormones from overseas, friends, or the internet. A 22-year-old transgender woman from Indonesia explained, I cannot get any access from medical providers, so I just read about it on the internet. Most transgender people are self-medicating too. It’s rare to find trans women who deal with doctors for hormone replacement therapy. Concerns about the potential harmful side effects of prolonged hormone use were widespread. A 29-year-old transgender woman from Brazil expressed worry about the quality of illicit hormones and the high costs of accessing high-quality hormones. An HIV-positive transgender woman stopped hormone use due to a lack of medical supervision and fear of health complications. The lack of access to gender-affirming surgery through public healthcare systems was another significant barrier. Long waiting lists, arbitrary gatekeeping mechanisms, and the pathologizing nature of accessing such treatments deterred many individuals. A 29-year-old transgender woman from Brazil stated, The public healthcare system still pathologizes us. There’s a mandatory two-year psychological treatment requirement, and there’s a long waiting line for surgery. Some individuals sought private options for surgery, but the high costs were a major obstacle. A 29-year-old transgender man from Singapore shared, I had to take on a loan to get my surgery because I just wanted to get it over with and move on with my life. Many respondents expressed distrust in the technical ability of medical professionals and the quality of gender-affirming surgeries, whether publicly or privately financed. Concerns about post-surgery complications, financial hardships, and increased HIV-related risks were also raised. A 31-year-old transgender woman from South Africa questioned, What are the risks of having sex with a surgically created vagina? Despite these challenges, some transgender individuals emphasized the importance of surgery for their psychological well-being. A 31-year-old transgender man from the United States reflected, Having breast removal surgery was amazing. It allowed me to recognize myself in the mirror. Supportive factors included financial resources to afford private surgery or travel abroad, often to countries like Thailand, where high-quality surgeries were available. Peer support and knowledge-sharing within the transgender community were also critical in overcoming barriers. A 27-year-old transgender man from Singapore described, A group of us decided to experiment together. We learned from each other and gained control over our hormone dosages, something doctors here wouldn’t allow. To improve access to hormone therapy and surgery, many interviewees suggested training healthcare professionals to competently address gender transition issues and provide recommendations for safer self-administered hormone use. Reducing gatekeeping mechanisms and psychological assessments was also seen as essential. A 30-year-old transgender woman from South Africa stated, We need to educate healthcare professionals so they understand how to distribute hormones and know they are allowed to do it. These findings highlight the need for global guidance on gender-affirming treatments and surgery, as well as appropriate training and capacity-building to make these services more widely available.
